description: Somos integrantes del semillero de investigación BIOMIND de Ingeniería Biomédica de la Fundación Universitaria del Área Andina. Nos apasionan la investigación, la innovación y el desarrollo de soluciones en el área de la salud. Buscamos personas comprometidas, creativas, curiosas y con iniciativa, que quieran aportar sus conocimientos, aprender y trabajar en equipo para generar proyectos con impacto.
summary: We developed AURA (Autonomous Universal Risk Analyzer), a modular wearable health monitor for astronauts based on the ESP32 microcontroller. It integrates biomedical and environmental sensors: electrocardiogram (AD8232), optical pulse (XD-58C), body temperature (PTC100), cabin temperature and humidity (DHT11), and ionizing radiation (M4011 Geiger tube), with immediate feedback on an OLED screen and an acoustic alarm (buzzer). Built around the hazards NASA identifies for human spaceflight—especially radiation, hostile closed environments, and distance from Earth—AURA classifies every reading with a traffic light (normal, caution, critical alert) and tells the astronaut what to do without waiting for contact with Earth. A web simulation shows the same logic with a live ECG, the OLED screen, and the buzzer. This matters because on deep-space missions, communication delays prevent immediate medical help from Earth, so AURA supports the astronaut's autonomy in spotting arrhythmias, thermal stress, or critical radiation exposure early.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

THE PROBLEM

On long missions, astronauts face space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. With distance from Earth, they carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves, and they cannot wait for ground contact. The challenge asks for software that gathers health indicators and lets astronauts evaluate and act on them. AURA's idea is that the astronaut should not only see numbers, but understand them and know what to do.

WHAT AURA DOES

AURA is a modular wearable health monitor (ESP32 plus sensors) with a web simulation. It follows four steps:

  1. Sense: the ESP32 reads the cardiac sensors (AD8232 ECG with electrodes RA, LA, and RL, and XD-58C optical pulse), body temperature (PTC100 in the armpit), habitat temperature and humidity (DHT11), and radiation (M4011 Geiger tube).
  2. Classify: each variable is compared with reference ranges and labeled normal (green), caution (yellow), or critical alert (red). The overall state is the worst of all variables, and a state changes only when a variable stays in the new range for about 10 seconds.
  3. Show: an OLED screen displays live values and status.
  4. Alert and guide: a caution gives a visible warning and a short beep; a critical alert blinks the screen and sounds the buzzer, and the protocol states the action: shelter, stop activity, re-measure, or notify the medical officer or Mission Control. If two critical alerts happen at once, radiation is handled first, sensor faults are ruled out, and Mission Control is notified with the time, values, and actions taken.

HOW IT IS WORN

The user cleans the torso, places the ECG electrodes (RA below the right collarbone, LA below the left, RL on the lower right ribs), the pulse sensor on the index fingertip, and the temperature sensor in the armpit, and mounts the ESP32, DHT11, and Geiger tube on the shoulder (DHT11 ventilated, tube uncovered). After powering on, the astronaut stays still for 10 seconds until the OLED confirms the ECG baseline.

REFERENCE RANGES (EXAMPLES)

  • Radiation: normal below 0.2 µSv/h, caution 0.2 to 0.5, critical above 0.5.
  • Heart rate: normal 60 to 100 bpm, critical below 50 or above 115 on both sensors.
  • Body temperature: normal 36.0 to 37.5 °C, critical at 38.5 °C or above, or 35.0 °C or below.
  • Habitat temperature: normal 18 to 24 °C.
  • Habitat humidity: normal 30 to 60%.

HONEST SIGNALS

A loose electrode (flagged by the AD8232's LO+ and LO- pins) shows CHECK SENSOR in gray, so a technical fault is not confused with a medical emergency.

WEB SIMULATION

A web page shows how AURA would behave without a real emergency: a live synthetic ECG next to a model of the OLED screen, the traffic light, and the buzzer. The user picks one of six hypothetical cases (normal, agitation, radiation caution, radiation alert, cardiac alert, loose electrode) and the data changes according to the protocol ranges. The same thresholds drive the device and the simulation.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Autonomy in deep space: it guides the astronaut on what to do without waiting for ground contact.
  • Readable at a glance: traffic-light colors plus text, never color alone, with simple explanations for people who are not experts.
  • Clear actions: every alert comes with a short protocol (what to do in caution, in critical alert, and when to call for help).
  • Honest signals: sensor faults are separated from medical alerts, which avoids false emergencies.
  • Context: habitat temperature and humidity appear next to body temperature and heart rate, so the astronaut can compare them before acting.
  • Two readings for the heart: ECG and optical pulse are combined, and a critical heart-rate alert requires both sensors.
  • Hardware and software together: the web simulation lets anyone, including a jury or a trainee, try the logic safely.

What is the expected impact of the project?

AURA aims to help crews detect problems earlier, such as cardiovascular stress, heat or cold stress, humidity problems in the habitat, and overexposure to radiation, and to act before a situation becomes critical. By turning measurements into a traffic light and a clear action, it supports the astronaut's decisions during long missions, when help from Earth is delayed. Its low-cost, modular design could also be adapted to terrestrial settings with extreme conditions or limited access to specialists.

AURA is a challenge prototype, not a medical device. Its ranges are the team's reference values and still need validation with clinical literature, NASA sources, and flight-surgeon guidance.

NEXT STEPS

  • Fix and test the pin assignments on the board.
  • Calibrate the PTC100 conversion and the Geiger counts-to-µSv/h factor.
  • Add entry for blood pressure, blood sugar, daily sleep hours, and mood.
  • Add trend charts, periodic measurement reminders, and optional gamification.
  • Connect the web interface to the real device so the simulation becomes a live dashboard.
  • Extend thresholds for different settings (spacecraft, station, rover, planetary base).

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

  • Hardware: ESP32; AD8232 ECG module with three electrodes (RA, LA, RL); XD-58C optical pulse sensor; PTC100 temperature sensor; DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor; M4011 Geiger tube; OLED display; buzzer.
  • Software: embedded code for the ESP32 (signal reading, pulse counting, display, and alerts), and a self-contained web page in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the simulation (live synthetic P-Q-R-S-T ECG, traffic-light logic, OLED model, optional buzzer), hosted on Tencent EdgeOne. Claude (by Anthropic) was used to help develop the simulator's functioning (see Use of AI).
  • Documentation: manufacturer datasheets for each sensor and NASA Human Research Program resources.

In what sense is your project creative?

AURA does not only display numbers: it turns every reading into a traffic light and a clear action, and the same logic runs on the device and in the web simulation. It treats technical faults honestly (CHECK SENSOR in gray), requires both cardiac sensors to agree before a critical heart alert, and prioritizes radiation when two alerts happen at once.

The simulation lets anyone try the logic without a real emergency, with a live ECG, an OLED model, and a buzzer, and the sound is optional. We also compared rest and agitation in four people to prepare the calibration of the alerts, linking the design to real measurements of how the body responds.

What factors did your team take into account?

  • NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments.
  • Communication delay with Earth: a three-state traffic light with visual and acoustic feedback and a written protocol, so the astronaut is guided without ground intervention.
  • Individual physiological variability: we measured pulse, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure in four people, first at rest and then while agitated. Pulse rose between +2% and +45%, systolic pressure between 0% and +27%, and saturation changed between -4% and +6%. The sample is small, so the results illustrate the method rather than support general conclusions.
  • Hardware integrity: the ECG's LO+ and LO- pins detect electrode detachment, the DHT11 must stay ventilated, and the Geiger tube uncovered.
  • Readability: color plus text, so the status is understood at a glance and does not depend on color alone.
  • Limits: not a medical device, ranges to be validated, small sample, and hypothetical data in the simulation.
